heroIntro: Entering into a partnership firm begins with shared commercial ambitions and mutual trust. However, when a managing partner begins siphoning revenues into personal bank accounts, concealing transaction books, or operating parallel competing businesses, the firm faces imminent financial ruin and bitter legal warfare.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: Legal Remedies When a Partner Siphons Firm Funds
quickAnswer.text: Under the Partnership Act 1932, partners owe absolute fiduciary fidelity and must account for all business earnings. If a managing partner embezzles funds or conceals ledger books, an aggrieved partner can file a Suit for Dissolution and Rendition of Accounts in the Joint District Judge Court, seek the immediate appointment of a Court Receiver under Order XL CPC, secure an injunction under Order XXXIX CPC, and lodge criminal cases under Sections 406 and 420 of the Penal Code.

sections.title: The Anatomy of Partnership Breakdowns in Bangladesh
sections.content:
Imagine investing tens of lakhs of taka into a promising commercial partnership in Dhaka, Chattogram, or Narayanganj—perhaps an import-export trading concern, an IT agency, or a readymade garments manufacturing unit. As an investing partner, you relied on the managing partner to supervise daily operations, maintain billing records, and manage commercial banking channels.

Over time, revenue distributions mysteriously dry up. The managing partner claims market downturns and heavy operational losses, yet arrives in luxury vehicles and acquires prime residential plots. When you demand to inspect the firm's ledgers and bank statements, you are stonewalled, physically barred from the office premises, or threatened with false criminal litigation.

This betrayal is one of the most destructive commercial disputes in Bangladesh. However, the legal system does not permit a dishonest partner to hide behind informal accounting tricks. The Partnership Act 1932 and the Code of Civil Procedure provide comprehensive, coercive tools to audit stolen funds, freeze corporate assets, appoint independent court receivers, and hold rogue partners criminally responsible.

sections.title: Fiduciary Duties Under the Partnership Act 1932
sections.content:
Under the Partnership Act 1932, the relationship between partners is fundamentally rooted in uberrima fides—the highest standard of good faith and mutual fiduciary duty. The Act establishes several non-negotiable statutory mandates:

  • General Duties of Partners (Section 9): Partners are bound to carry on the business of the firm to the greatest common advantage, to be just and faithful to each other, and to render true accounts and full information of all things affecting the firm.
  • Duty to Indemnify for Fraud (Section 10): Every partner must indemnify the firm for any loss caused to it by their fraud in the conduct of the business of the firm.
  • Accountability for Personal Profits (Section 16(a)): If a partner derives any personal profit for themselves from any transaction of the firm, or from the use of the property or business connection of the firm or the firm name, they are legally bound to account for that profit and pay it into the firm.
  • Prohibition on Competing Businesses (Section 16(b)): If a partner carries on any business of the same nature as and competing with that of the firm without consent, they must account for and surrender all profits made in that competing business.

Any managing partner who secretly diverts clients or revenues into a side enterprise commits a direct statutory breach of Section 16.

sections.title: Investigating and Documenting Fund Misappropriation
sections.content:
Before rushing into court, an aggrieved partner must systematically build an airtight evidentiary portfolio. Courts decide commercial disputes on verifiable paper trails, not emotional accusations:

  1. Banking and Transactional Forensics: Obtain copies of the firm's official bank account statements. Compare incoming payments from major clients against the invoices recorded in company books. Trace electronic transfers routed to the personal accounts of the managing partner or their relatives.
  2. VAT and Tax Reconciliation: Scrutinize the firm's monthly VAT Mushak 6.3 invoices and annual income tax returns filed with the National Board of Revenue (NBR). Discrepancies between declared taxable turnover and actual sales records provide conclusive proof of suppressed revenue.
  3. Digital Communications and Audit Records: Preserve all email correspondence, WhatsApp chats, vendor delivery challans, and signed internal vouchers confirming operational transactions and disputed asset purchases.

Serving a formal Advocate Legal Notice demanding access to the firm's books under Section 12(d) of the Partnership Act establishes a statutory record of non-compliance if the managing partner refuses access.

sections.title: Suit for Dissolution and Rendition of Accounts (Section 44)
sections.content:
When negotiations fail and the partnership is hopelessly compromised, the definitive civil remedy is filing a Suit for Dissolution of Partnership and Rendition of Accounts in the Joint District Judge Court under Section 44 of the Partnership Act 1932.

Section 44 empowers the civil court to dissolve a partnership firm upon the petition of a partner on several statutory grounds:

  • Section 44(c) - Prejudicial Misconduct: Where a partner is guilty of conduct which is calculated to prejudicially affect the carrying on of the business.
  • Section 44(d) - Persistent Breach of Agreement: Where a partner willfully or persistently commits breach of agreements relating to the management of the firm or conducts themselves such that it is not reasonably practicable for the other partners to carry on business with them.
  • Section 44(g) - Just and Equitable Grounds: The court possesses broad equitable discretion to dissolve a firm whenever circumstances render continued partnership impossible.

Upon hearing the preliminary stage, the court pronounces a Preliminary Decree for Accounts, appointing a qualified Advocate Commissioner or Chartered Accountant to examine all ledgers, determine total misappropriated funds, and submit a formal audit report to the court.

sections.title: Injunctive Relief and Freezing Firm Bank Accounts
sections.content:
The moment a rogue partner realizes a lawsuit has been filed, their instinctive reaction is often to empty company bank accounts, liquidate warehouse stock at distressed prices, and transfer machinery to third parties. Preventing this dissipation requires immediate injunctive relief.

Under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, your legal counsel must file an urgent application for an ad-interim temporary injunction concurrently with the plaint:

  • Restraining Bank Withdrawals: Impleading the firm's commercial banks as pro-forma defendants and seeking a restraining order against the rogue partner operating the accounts unilaterally.
  • Restraining Disposal of Firm Assets: Prohibiting the sale, mortgage, or transfer of factory premises, machinery, vehicles, patents, or trade inventories.
  • Maintaining Status Quo: Freezing existing commercial operations to preserve the firm's capital until the court adjudicates the preliminary decree.

Securing an injunction immediately shifts leverage back to the aggrieved partner, forcing the wrongdoer to the negotiating table.

sections.title: Order XL CPC: Appointment of a Court Receiver
sections.content:
In severe disputes where partners are physically fighting or where the managing partner continues to embezzle daily cash flows, an injunction alone may be insufficient. The ultimate protective measure is the Appointment of a Receiver under Order XL Rule 1 CPC.

Where it appears to the court to be 'just and convenient,' the Joint District Judge has statutory power to appoint a Court Receiver to take immediate physical custody and management of the partnership business:

  1. Seizure of Books and Assets: The Receiver immediately enters the firm's offices, seizes all physical ledgers, servers, chequebooks, and keys to warehouses.
  2. Neutral Day-to-Day Management: The Receiver oversees ongoing operations, collects outstanding debts from clients, pays staff salaries, and deposits all operational revenues into a dedicated court-supervised bank account.
  3. Exclusion of Rogue Partners: The delinquent partner is stripped of administrative authority and physically excluded from handling company money.

Bangladeshi courts readily appoint receivers in partnership disputes where prima facie evidence of gross financial diversion and waste of assets is presented.

sections.title: Criminal Remedies: Sections 406, 409, and 420 Penal Code
sections.content:
While partnership disputes are primarily civil matters, siphoning firm money frequently crosses the boundary into serious criminal offenses under the Penal Code 1860:

  • Section 406 Penal Code (Criminal Breach of Trust): A partner is an agent of the firm and holds company funds in a fiduciary capacity. If a partner dishonestly misappropriates or converts to their own use money belonging to the partnership, they are punishable with imprisonment for up to 3 years, or fine, or both.
  • Section 409 Penal Code (Criminal Breach of Trust by Banker, Merchant, or Agent): Where the partner acted as a managing agent or commercial trustee, penalties extend up to 10 years or life imprisonment.
  • Section 420 Penal Code (Cheating and Dishonestly Inducing Delivery of Property): Applicable where a partner induced investments based on fabricated profit projections or false capital contributions, carrying up to 7 years imprisonment.
  • Section 477A Penal Code (Falsification of Accounts): Penalizes any partner who willfully alters, mutilates, or falsifies firm account books with intent to defraud.

Filing a Complaint Register (CR) case before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or Thana FIR creates intense criminal liability that accelerates settlement.

sections.content:

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Recovering Misappropriated Capital in Dhaka
sections.content:
Illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed): Kamrul and Navid established a partnership logistics firm in Motijheel, Dhaka, with a registered deed specifying equal 50-50 shareholding. Kamrul invested BDT 50 Lakh in cash, while Navid managed daily fleet operations. By the end of 2025, Navid claimed the company was running at a steep loss, demanding that Kamrul inject an additional BDT 20 Lakh to maintain vehicle leases.

Suspicious of the sudden deficit, Kamrul covertly engaged an independent forensic accountant. An audit revealed that Navid had opened a secret bank account under a nearly identical trade name in Uttara, diverting corporate transport contracts worth BDT 85 Lakh directly into his private account, while using Kamrul's capital to cover fuel and repair expenses.

Kamrul's advocate immediately moved the Joint District Judge Court with a Suit for Dissolution and Rendition of Accounts, concurrently filing an application for an ad-interim injunction and the appointment of a Court Receiver. Concurrently, a CR case under Section 406/420 Penal Code was lodged before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court.

The civil judge promptly granted an injunction freezing the firm's commercial accounts and issued a show-cause notice for a Receiver. Facing criminal arrest warrants and frozen operational cash flows, Navid conceded, signing a formal Solenama (compromise agreement) returning BDT 65 Lakh to Kamrul and dissolving the partnership peacefully.

faqs.q: Can an unregistered partnership firm file a suit for accounts in Bangladesh?
faqs.a: Under Section 69(1) and (2) of the Partnership Act 1932, an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties or enforce contractual claims. However, Section 69(3)(a) provides an explicit exception: any partner can sue for the dissolution of the firm and for the rendition of accounts of a dissolved firm, regardless of whether the firm is registered with RJSC.

faqs.q: Can a partner be held criminally liable for stealing firm money under Section 406 Penal Code?
faqs.a: Yes. While partners hold joint ownership of assets, when a partner is entrusted with specific funds or books and dishonestly misappropriates them for personal enrichment to the exclusion of other partners, the Supreme Court has affirmed that criminal prosecution under Section 406 and 420 Penal Code is fully maintainable.

faqs.q: How does the court determine the exact share of profits if the partnership deed is silent?
faqs.a: Under Section 13(b) of the Partnership Act 1932, in the absence of any contract to the contrary, all partners are presumed to be entitled to share equally in the profits earned and must contribute equally to the losses sustained by the firm, regardless of differing capital contributions.

faqs.q: What happens to the partnership assets and liabilities upon court-ordered dissolution?
faqs.a: Under Section 48 of the Partnership Act, upon dissolution, firm assets are applied first to pay the debts and liabilities of the firm to third parties, second to repay advances made by partners beyond capital, third to pay each partner rateably what is due to them for capital, and any surplus is divided among partners in profit-sharing proportions.

faqs.q: Can the court appoint a Receiver before the final judgment of the dissolution lawsuit?
faqs.a: Yes. Under Order XL Rule 1 CPC, the court can appoint an interim Receiver at any stage of the proceedings, even immediately after the suit is filed, if the applicant demonstrates a strong prima facie case of fund diversion, asset dissipation, or gross mismanagement.

faqs.q: What is the time limit for an expelled or retired partner to file a suit for accounts?
faqs.a: Under Article 106 of the Limitation Act 1908, a suit for an account and a share of the profits of a dissolved partnership must be filed strictly within 3 years from the date of the dissolution of the firm.

faqs.q: Can an aggrieved partner freeze the firm's bank accounts immediately through an injunction?
faqs.a: Yes. By submitting bank statements, partnership deeds, and evidence of unauthorized personal withdrawals, your advocate can petition the Joint District Judge Court under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 CPC for an ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining the banks from honoring cheques signed unilaterally by the rogue partner.

faqs.q: What happens if a partner secretly starts a competing business using firm trade secrets?
faqs.a: Under Section 16(b) of the Partnership Act 1932, any partner who operates a competing business of the same nature without the consent of the other partners is statutorily obligated to account for and surrender all personal profits derived from that competing enterprise to the original firm.
